title: Embedding Models: Representations, Similarity & Fine-tuning — Audio Guide

chapters.title: Mental Model
chapters.script: Think of an embedding model as a learned compressor whose only job is to make semantically close items geometrically close. It takes variable-length text and maps it to a fixed-length vector so that a similarity metric like cosine or dot product on those vectors approximates human judgment of relatedness for the task it was trained on. That last clause is critical: an embedding space is not universal. It is shaped by its contrastive training objective, so a model tuned for symmetric similarity between sentence pairs behaves differently from one tuned for asymmetric retrieval where a short query has to match a long passage. Choosing and tuning an embedding model means choosing which notion of similarity gets baked into the geometry. Everything downstream, including vector search, retrieval-augmented generation retrieval quality, deduplication, and clustering, is just geometry on that space.

chapters.title: Words to Vectors
chapters.script: The central insight behind text embeddings is simple: map text into a continuous vector space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. What makes modern embedding models powerful is the quality of this mapping. Early approaches like TF-IDF and BM25 represented documents as sparse vectors over vocabulary terms. They worked well for lexical matching but failed to capture synonymy or compositional meaning. Word2Vec showed that neural networks trained on word co-occurrence could learn dense vectors where semantic relationships emerged as linear directions in the space, famously king minus man plus woman equals queen. But word-level embeddings could not capture polysemy or sentence-level meaning. The transformer revolution, beginning with BERT, enabled contextual representations where each token's embedding depends on its surrounding context. Yet BERT's native outputs produced surprisingly poor sentence embeddings out of the box. Sentence-BERT addressed this with a siamese network architecture: a pretrained transformer encodes two sentences independently, and a pooling operation, typically mean pooling over token embeddings, produces fixed-size sentence vectors. The key innovation was the training objective. Instead of fine-tuning with cross-attention between sentence pairs, which is effective but computationally prohibitive for search, Sentence-BERT optimizes the pooled representations directly. This enables efficient similarity computation at inference time. You encode each document once, store those vectors, then at query time encode the query and compute similarity against all document vectors, accelerated with approximate nearest neighbor algorithms.

chapters.title: Contrastive Learning
chapters.script: Modern embedding models are predominantly trained with contrastive learning objectives borrowed from computer vision. The core idea is to pull representations of semantically similar pairs closer together while pushing dissimilar pairs apart. The most common training objective is InfoNCE, noise contrastive estimation. For a batch of positive pairs, all other documents in the batch serve as negatives. This in-batch negatives strategy is remarkably efficient: a batch of 1024 pairs provides 1023 negatives per query for free. A temperature parameter controls the sharpness of the distribution. Too high and the model fails to discriminate; too low and gradient signal vanishes for most negatives. Not all negatives are equally useful. Random negatives provide little learning signal, so hard negatives, documents that are superficially similar but not actually relevant, force the model to learn finer-grained distinctions. Effective strategies for hard negative mining include retrieving lexically similar but semantically irrelevant documents using BM25, using a more powerful cross-encoder to identify hard negatives, selecting the highest-scoring negatives within each batch, or mining from previous model checkpoints. Modern high-performing embedding models typically follow a multi-stage training pipeline: large-scale weakly supervised contrastive learning on naturally occurring text pairs, followed by supervised contrastive learning on curated labeled pairs with hard negatives, and optionally distillation where smaller models learn to mimic the similarity scores of larger cross-encoder teachers. Models like BGE, the BAAI General Embedding, exemplify this approach.

chapters.title: Similarity Metrics
chapters.script: The choice of similarity metric defines the geometry of semantic comparison. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude. It is the most commonly used metric for text embeddings because it is magnitude-invariant: a longer document and a shorter document expressing the same idea will have high similarity regardless of vector norms. The dot product incorporates both direction and magnitude. When vectors are L2 normalized, they are unit length, and dot product equals cosine similarity. Some models, like those from OpenAI, return normalized vectors, making the distinction moot. Unnormalized dot product can be useful when magnitude encodes relevance signal. Euclidean distance, or L2 distance, measures straight-line distance in the embedding space. For normalized vectors, minimizing L2 distance is equivalent to maximizing cosine similarity. Euclidean distance is less common for text retrieval but appears in some clustering applications. The critical insight is to always match the metric to what the model was trained with. Using Euclidean distance on a model trained to optimize cosine similarity will produce suboptimal results, even though the ranking may be similar for normalized vectors.

chapters.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
chapters.script: A significant practical challenge with embeddings is the trade-off between dimensionality and performance. Higher dimensions capture more information but increase storage costs and slow similarity computation. Matryoshka Representation Learning, introduced by Kusupati and colleagues, offers an elegant solution. It trains embedding models so that the first d dimensions of a D-dimensional embedding form a useful d-dimensional embedding on their own. Like Russian nesting dolls, representations at multiple granularities are nested within a single vector. The training objective modifies the standard contrastive loss to optimize at multiple dimensionalities simultaneously. The impact is substantial. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large, with 3072 dimensions, can be truncated to 256 dimensions with only around four percent degradation on retrieval benchmarks. This means a twelve-fold reduction in vector database size, proportional speedup in similarity computation, and flexibility to choose dimensionality based on accuracy-cost trade-off per use case.

chapters.title: MTEB Benchmark
chapters.script: The Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, known as MTEB, provides a comprehensive evaluation framework spanning eight task categories and over fifty-eight datasets. Understanding MTEB is essential for informed model selection. The categories include retrieval, semantic textual similarity, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, summarization, and cross-lingual bitext mining. Aggregate MTEB scores can be misleading because a model that excels at semantic similarity may underperform on retrieval, and vice versa. For retrieval-augmented generation applications, focus on retrieval performance using metrics like normalized discounted cumulative gain at ten on datasets such as MS MARCO and Natural Questions. Domain mismatch is critical: MTEB datasets are predominantly general-domain English, so performance on specialized domains like legal, medical, or code may differ dramatically. Compare models at the same dimensionality for fair assessment, and consider inference speed because a model with two percent higher MTEB but ten times slower inference may not be the right choice.

chapters.title: Current Model Landscape
chapters.script: The embedding model landscape includes both proprietary and open-source options. OpenAI offers text-embedding-3-large with 3072 dimensions and Matryoshka truncation, priced at about thirteen cents per million tokens, and a smaller more cost-effective variant. Cohere's embed-v3 provides 1024 dimensions with strong multilingual support across over one hundred languages and uses an input type parameter to adapt representations. BGE from BAAI is open-source and self-hostable, with models like bge-large-en-v1.5 competitive with proprietary offerings. The E5 family, pioneered by Wang and colleagues, demonstrated the importance of training data curation, with larger backbones like a 7 billion parameter model achieving top MTEB scores but at significant computational cost. GTE, or General Text Embeddings, built on the Qwen2 backbone, supports 8192 token context. Nomic Embed is fully open-source, including training code and data, supports Matryoshka truncation down to 64 dimensions, and has a multimodal companion model sharing the same embedding space. Voyage AI offers domain-specific variants optimized for code, law, and finance, and is recommended by Anthropic for Claude-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. Jina Embeddings v3 uses task-specific LoRA adapters that modify model weights rather than consuming input tokens, avoiding context-length overhead. Beyond the original MTEB, version 2 expanded evaluation to over 250 languages, long-document retrieval, and instruction following. Domain-specific leaderboards for legal, biomedical, and code retrieval often reveal surprising rank inversions, so evaluating on your own domain is more predictive than aggregate scores.

chapters.title: Fine-Tuning with Synthetic Data
chapters.script: Off-the-shelf embedding models often underperform on domain-specific data. Fine-tuning with task-specific data is the standard remedy, but labeled data is expensive. Synthetic data generation offers a practical path forward. You can use a large language model to generate synthetic queries from your documents. For each document, you ask the model to produce several diverse questions that the document would answer. This gives you query-document pairs for training. Then using a library like SentenceTransformers, you load a base model and prepare training examples. The MultipleNegativesRankingLoss implements in-batch negatives. A few key considerations: do not over-fine-tune because embedding models can catastrophically forget general knowledge. Use a low learning rate, typically between one and five times ten to the minus five, and only one to five epochs. Batch size matters because larger batches provide more in-batch negatives. Use gradient accumulation if GPU memory is limited; a batch size of 256 or more is ideal. Evaluate on held-out data using retrieval metrics like nDCG at ten or recall at k to detect overfitting. Mining hard negatives from BM25 or a previous model checkpoint dramatically improves fine-tuning effectiveness.

chapters.title: Learned Sparse Representations
chapters.script: While dense embeddings dominate, learned sparse representations combine the interpretability of lexical methods like BM25 with the semantic understanding of neural models. SPLADE, which stands for Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model, is the most prominent approach. It uses a transformer encoder to produce a sparse vector over the entire vocabulary. For each input token, the model predicts activation weights across all vocabulary terms. Crucially, it can activate terms that do not appear in the input text. This term expansion gives SPLADE its semantic power: a document about automobile recalls can activate the term car even if that word never appears. Sparsity is enforced through a regularization penalty that limits the total number of activated terms, typically resulting in one hundred to three hundred non-zero entries out of a thirty-thousand-plus vocabulary. The output can be stored in traditional inverted indexes alongside BM25, avoiding the need for a separate vector database. Learned sparse representations have distinct advantages in entity-heavy queries where dense embeddings struggle with rare proper nouns, in interpretability requirements where you can inspect which terms contributed to a match, and in out-of-domain robustness where the lexical component provides a reliable fallback. SPLADE is not a replacement for dense embeddings but a complementary signal. Hybrid retrieval strategies that combine dense and sparse scores are common in production systems.

chapters.title: Multimodal Embeddings
chapters.script: The embedding paradigm extends naturally beyond text. Multimodal embedding models map different modalities, including text, images, audio, and video, into a shared vector space where cross-modal similarity becomes meaningful. CLIP, Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, established the foundational approach. It jointly trains a text encoder and an image encoder using contrastive learning on four hundred million image-caption pairs. The training objective is identical in spirit to InfoNCE: within each batch, the model pulls matching image-caption pairs together and pushes non-matching pairs apart. The result is a shared embedding space where a photo of a golden retriever and the text a photo of a golden retriever occupy nearby regions. This enables cross-modal retrieval, zero-shot classification, and multimodal retrieval-augmented generation where systems can surface images, diagrams, or charts alongside text passages. SigLIP refines the approach by using a sigmoid loss per pair instead of softmax, making training more efficient. OpenCLIP provides fully open weights, while Jina CLIP v2 extends the architecture to multilingual text. Nomic Embed Vision aligns visual and textual embeddings with full Matryoshka support. Deploying multimodal embeddings introduces challenges: image encoders are substantially more expensive to run than text encoders, so pre-computing image embeddings during ingestion is critical. The embedding dimensionality must be shared across modalities, and the semantic granularity differs, with text queries often expressing rich compositional detail that current vision encoders capture imperfectly.

chapters.title: Instruction-Prefixed Embeddings
chapters.script: A subtle but impactful development is the use of task-specific instruction prefixes that modify how the model produces representations. Rather than learning a single embedding function, these models condition the encoding on an explicit description of the intended task. The E5-instruct family pioneered this approach. At encoding time, each input is prepended with a natural language instruction describing the task. For example, for retrieval you might prepend the query with an instruction like given a web search query, retrieve relevant passages. The instruction tells the model what kind of similarity to optimize for. The same document encoded for a retrieval task and a clustering task may produce different embeddings. Different providers implement this in varying ways. E5-instruct accepts free-form instructions, offering maximum flexibility but risking degradation from poorly phrased instructions. BGE models use simpler fixed templates. Cohere embed-v3 abstracts the mechanism behind an input type parameter with options like search document, search query, classification, and clustering. Voyage AI focuses on query and document types for asymmetric retrieval. The effectiveness of instruction prefixes stems from the fundamental asymmetry in embedding tasks: queries are short and express information needs, while documents are long and express information content. A single embedding function must handle both sides, and the prefix provides explicit signal about which side is being encoded. Instruction-prefixed models show the largest gains on retrieval tasks, with three to five percent improvement in nDCG at ten on MTEB retrieval benchmarks, and smaller gains on symmetric tasks.

chapters.title: Practical Trade-Offs
chapters.script: Higher dimensionality captures more information but with diminishing returns. For cost-sensitive large-scale search, 256 dimensions might be used, requiring about one gigabyte per million vectors. General-purpose applications often use 768 to 1024 dimensions, needing three to four gigabytes. Maximum recall scenarios may use 1536 to 3072 dimensions, requiring six to twelve gigabytes. For most retrieval-augmented generation applications, 768 to 1024 dimensions provide the best accuracy-cost trade-off. With Matryoshka-trained models, you can start with lower dimensions and scale up if needed. Context length is another consideration. Embedding models have maximum context lengths ranging from 512 tokens for older models to over 8000 tokens for modern ones. However, longer inputs do not always produce better embeddings. The mean-pooling operation can dilute signal when averaging over many tokens. This is why chunking strategy is critical: how you split documents interacts directly with embedding quality.

chapters.title: Runtime Internals
chapters.script: The learned compressor model hides the mechanics that decide whether embeddings work in production. Contrastive training with in-batch negatives shapes the space efficiently. Embedding quality scales with batch size, which is why these models are trained on huge batches and why naive fine-tuning with tiny batches underperforms. Asymmetric retrieval requires instruction prefixes to put queries and documents in a comparable subspace. The runtime bug class is applying the wrong prefix or none at query time, which silently tanks recall while everything still runs. Prefix discipline must match index time and query time exactly. Matryoshka training allows you to store the full vector but search with a truncated prefix for a cheap first pass, then rerank with full dimensions. This is a coarse-to-fine speed and accuracy dial without re-embedding. Dense vectors capture semantics but miss exact terms; learned sparse representations like SPLADE expand terms and stay lexically precise. Many production systems run both in a hybrid approach. The dominant operational cost is versioning. Any model or prefix change invalidates the entire index, requiring a full re-embed. Embedding model upgrades are migrations, evaluated like a search relevance change, not configuration tweaks.
